n: News of Israel’s victories spreads to all the kings west of the Jordan — in the hill country, the lowlands, and along the Mediterranean coast.

f.g: The Shephelah — the low foothills toward the coast.

n: Normally rival city-states unite to fight Israel together.
But the people of Gibeon, a major city just a few miles from Ai, choose a different strategy.

f.g: A Hivite city about 6 miles (10 km) northwest of Jerusalem.

n: They act cleverly, disguising themselves as envoys from far away, with worn-out sacks and cracked, patched wineskins. The word “wilily” echoes Israel’s own trickery at Ai.
Worn and patched sandals, ragged clothes, and dry, crumbly bread complete the costume.
At Israel’s camp in Gilgal they claim to come from a distant land and ask for a treaty.

f.w: make ye a league with us

n: Israel is suspicious: what if you live nearby? The law forbade treaties with Canaanite peoples.

f.w: how shall we make a league with you

n: The Gibeonites humbly call themselves Joshua’s servants. Joshua asks directly who they are and where they’re from.
They say they came because of the fame of Israel’s God — mentioning only events far in the past, like Egypt, wisely leaving out recent Jericho and Ai.

f.w: because of the name of the LORD thy God

n: They mention the defeat of Sihon and Og east of the Jordan — old news a distant people might have heard.
They claim their elders sent them with provisions to offer submission and seek a treaty.
“This bread was warm from the oven when we left — look at it now.”
“These wineskins were new, and our clothes and shoes have worn out on the long journey.”

f.w: by reason of the very long journey
f.g: A clever lie supported by props.

n: Israel’s leaders sampled the provisions but did not ask the Lord for guidance — the critical mistake. Appearances can deceive; revelation does not.

f.w: asked not counsel at the mouth of the LORD

n: Joshua made peace with them, and the leaders swore an oath to spare their lives.
Three days later the truth came out: they were close neighbors.
Israel arrived at their four cities on the third day — all within a day’s march.

f.g: Later the resting place of the ark for twenty years.

n: Israel didn’t attack, because the leaders had sworn by the Lord. The people grumbled, but an oath in God’s name was binding.

f.w: sworn unto them by the LORD God of Israel

n: The leaders stood firm: we swore by the Lord, so we can’t harm them.
Breaking the oath would bring God’s wrath. Centuries later, when Saul violated it, Israel suffered famine.
Their lives were spared, but they became woodcutters and water carriers for the community.

f.w: hewers of wood and drawers of water

n: Joshua confronts them: Why did you deceive us?
Their consequence: permanent service — but in the house of God, for the sanctuary. A curse became a kind of blessing.

f.w: for the house of my God

n: Their honest answer: they knew God had commanded Israel to take the land, and they feared for their lives. Like Rahab, they believed God’s word.

f.w: we were sore afraid of our lives

n: They surrender completely: “We’re in your hands — do what seems right.”

f.w: as it seemeth good and right unto thee

n: Joshua protected them from Israelites who wanted to kill them.
They served at the Lord’s altar wherever he chose it — “unto this day.” Gibeon later became an important worship site where Solomon prayed for wisdom.

f.w: for the altar of the LORD
